# Cause of the seasons (tilted axis) (`seasons_axial_tilt`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: needs round_earth_size; helped by heliocentrism, sundial_water_clock
- Core idea: The seasons come from the tilt of the Earth's axis, about 23.5 degrees from the perpendicular to its orbital plane (in the older picture: the Sun's yearly path is inclined by that much to the celestial equator). In summer the Sun stands higher, its rays strike more steeply and the day is longer; in winter the reverse. Therefore the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres, the Sun passes overhead only between the tropics, and beyond about 66.5 degrees latitude there are days when it does not set. The tilt is measured from the noon shadow of a vertical pole at the two solstices: outside the tropics, where the Sun is above the horizon at both noons, half the difference between the two Sun heights.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying summer comes because the Earth is nearer the Sun; it is nearest in early January
  - Forgetting that the southern hemisphere has the opposite season
  - Saying the axis wobbles to and fro during the year; it keeps its direction
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1000 BC – MUL.APIN lists solstices, equinoxes and changing day length; china: gnomon shadow measurements of the solstices from the 1st millennium BC (Zhoubi suanjing); greece: 5th c. BC Oenopides credited with the obliquity; c. 240 BC Eratosthenes measures it as about 23 degrees 51 minutes; india: 499 – Aryabhata gives 24 degrees; islamic: 9th–10th c. – repeated measurements show the obliquity slowly decreasing; americas: solstice and zenith-passage alignments in Mesoamerican and Andean sites
- Read:
  - James Evans, The History and Practice of Ancient Astronomy (1998)
  - Otto Neugebauer, The Exact Sciences in Antiquity (1957)
